text: BASS aimed to begin bridging the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity.
quote: Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.

text: BASS assessed how well an inert gaseous extinguishing agent, similar to the one used on ISS, puts out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating and flow.
quote: Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.

text: BASS burned custom fabric samples of 75% cotton / 25% fiberglass by mass, plus Nomex fabric and Ultem.
quote: Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem.

text: In BASS the air flow along the sample reached up to 40 cm/s and could be opposed or concurrent to flame spread; the flow duct cross-section was 76 mm x 76 mm.
quote: The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric.

text: Current NASA spacecraft material selection (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) segregates materials on 1-g behavior without considering low-gravity effects.
quote: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects.

text: Using nitrogen as the flame suppressant in BASS links the results directly to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
quote: Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.

text: BASS microgravity flames were especially sensitive to air flow speed in the 0 to 5 cm/s range.
quote: Microgravity flames were found to be especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cms.

text: At the lowest flow speeds tested in BASS (below 1 cm/s) flames became dim blue and very stable and, with small heat loss, could burn for a long time.
quote: At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cms) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable. However, heat loss at these very low convective rates is small so the flames can burn for a long time.

text: Even the smallest BASS flames on acrylic slabs burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing, so a tiny flame might go undetected for a long time.
quote: Only the smallest flames burning acrylic slabs appeared to be adversely influenced by solid conductive heat loss, but even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing. This has implications for spacecraft fire safety since a tiny flame might be undetected for a long time.

text: A small, stable microgravity flame can flare up if air convection is suddenly increased or if it spreads into another fuel source.
quote: the danger is that it might flare up if the air convection is suddenly increased or if the flame spreads into another fuel source

text: In some BASS tests a jet of nitrogen was introduced to try to extinguish the flame.
quote: In some cases, a jet of nitrogen was introduced to attempt to extinguish the flame.

text: At moderate flow speeds (about 1 to 5 cm/s) the flame keeps heating the solid fuel, giving an increasingly strong, luminous flame over time.
quote: At moderate flow speeds (between about 1 and 5 cms) the flame continually heats the solid fuel resulting in an increasing fuel temperature, higher rate of fuel vaporization, and a stronger, more luminous flame as time progresses.

text: BASS-II objective: study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
quote: Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.

text: BASS-II aimed to begin bridging the gap between NASA-STD-6001 Test #1, ground-based microgravity tests and actual microgravity flammability.
quote: Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.

text: In BASS-II oxygen was varied only below 21% by adding nitrogen, and the wind tunnel imposed airflow up to 40 cm/s.
quote: Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen).

text: BASS-II tests the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well or better in microgravity than in normal gravity under otherwise identical conditions.
quote: BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity

text: NASA's upward-burning 1-g material test is considered worst case on Earth but may not be conservative for flammability in space.
quote:
NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for
flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space.

text: BASS-II flames are quite sensitive to air flow speed in the 0 to 5 cm/s range and can be sustained below 1 cm/s as dim blue, stable flames.
quote: The flames are quite sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cms. They can be sustained at very low flow speeds of less than 1 cms, when they become dim blue and stable.

text: Very-low-flow dim blue flames are not particularly dangerous but can flare up quickly with a sudden increase in air flow speed.
quote: In this state they are not particularly dangerous from a fire safety perspective, but they can flare up quickly with a sudden increase in air flow speed.

text: Including BASS-I, well over one hundred tests were run across geometries, flow speeds and oxygen concentrations; the BASS-II tunnel could impose flows up to 53 cm/s.
quote: Including earlier BASS-I results, well over one hundred tests have been conducted of the various samples in the different geometries, flow speeds, and oxygen concentrations.

text: For the SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric in concurrent flow, low-speed quenching extinction occurred at 1 to 5 cm/s, with higher quench speed at lower oxygen.
quote: The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher speed in lower oxygen atmosphere.

text: SIBAL fabric tests varied ambient oxygen from 21% down to 16% and flow from 40 cm/s down to 1 cm/s.
quote: Ambient oxygen was varied from 21% down to 16% and flow speed from 40 cm/s down to 1 cm/s.

text: Twenty-four concurrent-flow tests on cast PMMA rods mapped flammability limits as a function of oxygen and flow speed, finding both blowoff and quenching limits.
quote: Twenty-four concurrent-flow tests were performed, focusing on finding flammability limits as a function of oxygen and flow speed.

text: Quenching of PMMA rod flames occurred when the flow became too weak for the flame to offset conduction and radiation heat losses.
quote: Quenching was observed when the flow became sufficiently weak that the flame could no longer provide adequate heat flux to compensate for the heat losses (conduction into the rod and radiation).

text: On the blowoff branch the PMMA-rod flammability boundary depends linearly on oxygen concentration and stretch rate.
quote: For the blowoff branch, the boundary exhibits a linear dependence on oxygen concentration and stretch rate

text: Most BASS-II tests had heat release rates well below 100 W (from oxygen consumption, 13.1 kJ per gram O2).
quote: The results showed that most of the tests had heat release rates well below 100 W.

text: BASS-II was the first ISS experiment to dilute the glovebox working volume with gaseous N2 to reduce oxygen.
quote: For the first time on ISS, BASS–II utilized MSG working volume dilution with gaseous N2.

text: The global equivalence ratio of BASS-II tests was estimated as fuel rich, 1.3 on average.
quote: the global equivalence ratio for the tests is estimated to be fuel rich, 1.3 on average using mass loss and O2 consumption data

text: Normal-gravity blowoff limits for PMMA rods (0.635-3.81 cm, 14-18% O2) compare favorably with BASS-II when buoyant stretch and blockage are accounted for.
quote: These blowoff limits compare favorably with the BASS-II results when the buoyant stretch is included and the flow is corrected by considering the blockage factor of the fuel.

text: A proposed new 1-g upward flame spread test extrapolates the linear blowoff boundary to zero stretch to estimate microgravity flammability limits, which current methods cannot do.
quote: We describe a new normal gravity 'upward flame spread test' method which extrapolates the linear blowoff boundary to the zero stretch limit in order to resolve microgravity flammability limits-something current methods cannot do.

text: In 1-g the PMMA rod blowoff boundary is linear, with oxygen concentration directly proportional to flow speed.
quote: the normal gravity blowoff boundary for this axisymmetric rod geometry is determined to be linear, with oxygen concentration directly proportional to flow speed

text: Saffire-I burned a SIBAL (75% cotton / 25% fiberglass) sample about 0.94 m long and 0.4 m wide.
quote: The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric.

text: Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.
quote: Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.

text: Saffire objectives: determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's 1-g screening test.
quote:
(1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal
gravity material flammability screening test.

text: Saffire hypothesis: because fire behaves very differently in reduced gravity, designing spacecraft fire safety from terrestrial fires and standards carries inherent risk.
quote: the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty

text: Saffire was the first test of spacecraft fires at a scale relevant to real spacecraft.
quote: The Saffire Experiment represents the first test of spacecraft fires at a scale relevant to real spacecraft.

text: Saffire data resolved whether flame growth reaches a steady size and showed the enclosure around the sample affects flame spread more than anticipated.
quote: The downloaded test data show resolved the question of whether flame growth will achieve a steady size and demonstrated that the size of the enclosure surrounding the sample has more impact on the flame spread than anticipated.

text: Spacecraft fire spread and growth cannot be expected to scale linearly from small-scale test data.
quote: The spread and growth of a fire, combined with its interactions with the vehicle cannot be expected to scale linearly from small-scale test data

text: Before Saffire, microgravity fire experiments were limited to samples of order 10 cm in length and width or smaller.
quote: The major constraint has been the size of the sample, with prior experiments limited to samples of the order of 10 cm in length and width or smaller.

text: The lack of large-scale data forces spacecraft designers to base fire safety designs on 1-g understanding of flame spread, detection and suppression.
quote: This lack of experimental data forces spacecraft designers to base their designs and safety precautions on 1-g understanding of flame spread, fire detection, and suppression.

text: Saffire-1 and Saffire-3 were planned as flame spread tests of a meter-scale sample burned to completion inside the Cygnus pressurized volume.
quote: On two flights (Saffire-1 and Saffire-3), the experiment will consist of a flame spread test involving a meter-scale sample ignited in the pressurized volume of the spacecraft and allowed to burn to completion while measurements are made.

text: Low-gravity fire behaviour differs from normal gravity in flammability limits, ignition delay, flame spread, flame colour and structure.
quote: the work conducted to date has shown that fire behaviour in low-gravity is very different from that in normal-gravity, with differences observed for flammability limits, ignition delay, flame spread behaviour, flame colour and flame structure

text: The Saffire project's overall objective is to reduce the uncertainty and risk in designing spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA exploration missions.
quote: The overall objective of this project is to reduce the uncertainty and risk associated with the design of spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA's exploration missions.

text: Saffire tests are fully automated in Cygnus after it unberths from ISS, with data downlinked before reentry.
quote: The tests will be fully automated with the data downlinked at the conclusion of the test and before the Cygnus vehicle reenters the atmosphere.

text: Saffire-II carried 9 samples of 5 cm x 29 cm: SIBAL, silicone, structural PMMA, flat PMMA and PMMA with Nomex.
quote: Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm.

text: Saffire-II added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA and PMMA with Nomex.
quote: the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex

text: Depending on material, Saffire-II used 20 or 30 cm/s air flow, either concurrent or opposed.
quote: Depending on the sample material, the Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed.

text: Saffire-2 was designed to test 9 smaller (5 x 30 cm) samples to evaluate NASA's material flammability screening tests.
quote: On one of the flights (Saffire-2), 9 smaller (5 x 30 cm) samples will be tested to evaluate NASAs material flammability screening tests.

text: Pre-flight silicone samples for Saffire matched the NASA 6001 Test 1 geometry, 5 cm wide by 30 cm tall, in four thicknesses (0.25-1.00 mm).
quote: The sample geometry was chosen to match the NASA 6001 Test 1 specification, namely 5 cm wide by 30 cm tall.

text: In 1-g upward Test 1-style burns the silicone flame generally did not consume the whole sample; the thickest sample could not be ignited.
quote: In the upward buoyant flame spread tests, the flame generally did not burn the entire sample. As thickness was increased, the flame spread distance decreased before flame extinguishment. For the thickest sample, ignition could not be achieved.

text: Thin silicone samples burned completely in downward spread, an uncommon case where downward flames are more flammable than upward ones.
quote: The increased flammability for downward spreading flames relative to upward ones is uncommon.

text: Adding forced flow to upward silicone tests in air made them more flammable.
quote: Upward tests in air with an added forced flow were more flammable.

text: Saffire-II burned 10 mm thick PMMA in microgravity at 100 kPa with 200 mm/s air flow.
quote: Microgravity experiments were conducted during NASA’s Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire II), on board the Cygnus spacecraft at 100 kPa with an air flow velocity of 200 mm/s.

text: Reducing ambient pressure in 1-g slows concurrent flame spread over PMMA toward the microgravity rate, and the extrapolated correlation predicts the Saffire-II spread rate well.
quote: The extrapolation of the correlation to low pressures predicts well the flame spread rate obtained in microgravity in the Saffire II experiments.

text: Reduced-pressure ground tests can approximately replicate flame behavior of untested gravity conditions for thick and thin solids.
quote: Both results suggest that reduced pressure can be used to approximately replicate flame behavior of untested gravity conditions for the burning of thick and thin solids.

text: Saffire-III again burned SIBAL, but at 30 cm/s flow instead of Saffire-I's 20 cm/s.
quote: the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I

text: Saffire-III flows were either concurrent or opposed to flame spread.
quote: The flow was either concurrent or opposed.

text: Saffire-III instrumentation included thermocouples, two radiometers, pressure/CO2/O2 sensors and two anemometers.
quote: thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity

text: Saffire results are intended to determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials and help validate NASA's material selection criteria.
quote: Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size.

text: FLEX aimed to map liquid-fuel flammability limits in microgravity and measure the effectiveness of gaseous suppressants such as CO2, He and SF6.
quote: aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6

text: A primary FLEX objective was the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) versus ambient pressure and how a suppressant changes the LOI.
quote: A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

text: FLEX LOI tests were run at 0.5 to 1.5 atm with droplets of about 3 mm.
quote: Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests.

text: FLEX hypothesizes that absent buoyant convection, flammability limits and suppressant efficacy differ significantly from normal gravity.
quote: the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions

text: FLEX was to quantify the effect of different possible crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression and guide selection of the suppressant for next-generation crew vehicles.
quote: will assess the effectiveness of fire suppressants in microgravity and quantify the effect of different possible crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression

text: FLEX results were intended to direct large-scale fire suppression tests and the choice of fire suppressant for next-generation crew exploration vehicles.
quote: The goal of this research is to provide definition and direction for large scale fire suppression tests and selection of the fire suppressant for next generation crew exploration vehicles.

text: The limiting oxygen index for methanol droplets in CO2- or He-diluted gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.
quote: The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.

text: FLEX methanol tests used CO2 and helium dilution from 0% to 70% by volume at 0.7 and 1 atm.
quote: The inert dilution by carbon dioxide and helium varied over a range of 0% to 70% by volume.

text: FLEX methanol tests spanned ambient oxygen from 30% down to 12% by volume.
quote: The ambient oxygen concentration varied from a high value of 30% by volume to as low as 12%, approaching the limiting oxygen index for the fuel.

text: Droplets of 1.5-4 mm were used to capture both diffusive extinction and radiative extinction.
quote: The initial droplet size varied between approximately 1.5 mm and 4 mm to capture both diffusive extinction brought about by insufficient residence time at the flame and radiative extinction caused by excessive heat loss from the flame zone.

text: The FLEX detailed-results report presents the first 284 tests (March 2009 - December 2011).
quote: It also presents the results of the first 284 tests performed.

text: Large n-alkane droplets on ISS kept burning quasi-steadily in a low-temperature 'cool flame' regime after radiative extinction of the visible flame.
quote: large n-alkane droplets can continue to burn quasi-steadily following radiative extinction in a low-temperature regime, characterized by negative-temperaturecoefficient (NTC) chemistry

text: These n-alkane cool-flame tests used 14% to 25% oxygen at 1.0, 0.7 and 0.5 atm with CO2 or He diluents.
quote: The oxygen concentration in these tests varied in the range of 14% to 25% by volume.

text: ISS droplet experiments showed n-alkane fuels can sustain quasi-steady low-temperature combustion without any visible flame.
quote: normal-alkane fuels with negative temperature coefficient (NTC) chemistry can support quasi-steady, low-temperature combustion without any visible flame

text: FLEX research impacts include fire suppression in confined environments on Earth such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft.
quote: the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft

text: FLEX-2 extends FLEX-1 to fuels and conditions that mimic real combustors and provides benchmark data on bi-component droplet combustion.
quote: The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions

text: FLEX-2 varied chamber pressure from 0.5 to 3.0 atm and O2 from 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction.
quote: which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance

text: FLEX-2 studied how droplet interactions affect flammability limits and extinction of droplet arrays.
quote: Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays.

text: FLEX-2 independently varied fuel type, gas composition, pressure, droplet size, droplet translation velocity and array spacing.
quote: The independently varied experimental parameters during FLEX-2 experiments were 1) Fuel type 2) Ambient gas composition 3) Ambient Pressure 4) Droplet initial diameter 5) Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration) 6) Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.

text: Large n-decane/hexanol (50/50) droplets at elevated pressure showed a very weak visible flame but a relatively high burning rate, suggesting coexisting cool and hot flames.
quote: Recent experiments involving large, bi-component fuel (n-decane and hexanol, 50/50 by volume) droplets at elevated pressures show that the visible, hot flame becomes extremely weak while the burning rate remains relatively high

text: SAME's goal was to quantify the sizes liquid smoke particles reach in low gravity and relate them to smoke generation and transport conditions.
quote: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment.

text: SAME hypothesis: without buoyant flows, smoke from a pyrolyzing source grows larger particles in microgravity than in 1g.
quote: smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g

text: Changes in smoke size distribution in microgravity could cause some detectors not to alarm.
quote: The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

text: In SAME, the igniter heated samples for a predefined 15 to 60 seconds and each smoke event typically lasted 2 minutes.
quote: turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds)

text: All current spacecraft smoke detectors were designed for normal-g conditions because microgravity smoke data were absent.
quote: Owing to the absence of microgravity smoke data, all current spacecraft smoke detectors were designed based upon normal-g conditions.

text: Shuttle experiments confirmed that particle sizes can increase in low gravity and that relative ISS vs shuttle detector performance changes.
quote: Recent space shuttle experiments confirmed that, in some cases, increased particles sizes are seen in low-gravity and that the relative performance of the ISS (International Space Station) and space-shuttle smoke-detectors changes in low-gravity

text: The DAFT precursor found the ISS cabin very clean, with particulate levels far below the shuttle and typical ground environments.
quote: The ISS cabin was found to be a very clean environment with particulate levels substantially below the space shuttle and typical ground-based environments.

text: The ISS smoke detector uses forward light scattering in the near IR and is most sensitive to particles larger than 1 micron; the shuttle used an ionization detector, most sensitive to smaller particles.
quote: the ionization detector being most sensitive (on a mass concentration basis) to smaller particulate and the light scattering detector being most sensitive to particulate that is larger than 1 micron

text: Spacecraft fire detection targets pre-ignition pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer particles rather than soot.
quote: the target smoke for detection is typically not soot (typical of established hydrocarbon fires) but instead, pyrolysis products, and recondensed polymer particles

text: Shuttle and ISS smoke detection systems were designed without any data on low-gravity smoke or background dust size distributions.
quote: These two systems were designed in the absence of any data concerning low-gravity smoke particle (and background dust) size distributions.

text: In low gravity, negligible buoyant flow concentrates smoke near the source, increasing residence time and transport time to detectors.
quote: In low gravity, buoyant flow is negligible which causes particles to concentrate at the smoke source, increasing their residence time, and increasing the transport time to smoke detectors.

text: Given a spacecraft's fixed air volume, the primary detection target is pyrolysis products rather than soot, to catch fires before a flame is established.
quote: Consequently, the primary target for spacecraft fire detection is pyrolysis products rather than soot.

text: In the SAME reflight (Expedition 24, 2010) most average smoke particle sizes were 200-400 nm, with quiescent cases producing some substantially larger particles.
quote: Overall the majority of the average smoke particle sizes were found to be in the 200 nm to 400 nm range with the quiescent cases producing some cases with substantially larger particles.

text: SAME-R heated five spacecraft materials below ignition: Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell.
quote: Five different materials representative of those found in spacecraft (Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell) were heated to temperatures below the ignition point

text: Air flow past the SAME-R samples ranged from quiescent to 8 cm/s.
quote: The air flow past the sample during the heating period ranged from quiescent to 8 cm/s.

text: Smoke was aged 11 to 1800 s in a chamber to simulate transport time from source to detector.
quote: This effective transport time was varied by holding the smoke in the aging chamber for times ranging from 11 to 1800 s.

text: SAME-R included a prototype two-moment smoke detector among its diagnostics.
quote: The diagnostics included a prototype two-moment smoke detector and three different measures of moments of the particle size distribution.

text: SAME-R completed 66 test points from July 16 to September 9, 2010.
quote: SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points.

text: SAME-R added Pyrell intumescent foam, higher heating temperatures and no-flow heating, and the GRC M-pass instrument.
quote: Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples

text: The original SAME TEM grids were contaminated by unidentified foreign particles, making them unusable, which motivated SAME-R.
quote: all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable

text: SAME/SAME-R smoke detector results may also benefit extreme Earth environments such as submarines and underwater laboratories.
quote: The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories.

text: CFI examined n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane droplets at pressures from 0.25 to 5 atm and the effect of helium dilution on cool flames.
quote: Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.

text: CFI analyzed the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
quote: Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.

text: Cool-flame extinction diameter increases drastically with helium dilution compared with N2, CO2 or Xe; Xe dilution gives longer burning and smaller extinction diameter.
quote: The results show that the cool-flame extinction diameter is drastically increased with helium dilution compared to N2, CO2 or Xe, and Xe dilution leads to longer burning with a smaller extinction diameter.

text: Cool flames supporting droplet burning are not visible to the naked eye.
quote: These cool flames, not visible to the naked eye, result from the existence of the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) region

text: Cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet combustion was first observed on ISS in the Combustion Integrated Rack with n-alkane fuels.
quote: Cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet combustion was first observed during droplet combustion experiments conducted onboard the International Space Station (ISS) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) with n-alkane fuels.

text: Simulations show a near-quiescent n-heptane diffusion flame extinguishes at about 1200 K from radiative loss, then transitions to a cool flame near 700 K.
quote: a growing spherical diffusion flame extinguishes at ≈1200 K due to radiative heat losses. This is typically followed by a transition to the low-temperature (cool-flame) regime with a reaction zone (at ≈700 K) in close proximity to the fuel source

text: After about 18 s in the cool-flame regime, a flash re-ignition can occur.
quote: After a relatively long period (≈18 s) of the cool flame regime, a flash re-ignition occurs

text: Non-premixed cool flames were discovered during ISS droplet combustion research and later observed with gaseous fuel on a porous burner.
quote: Non-premixed cool flames were notably discovered during the droplet combustion research and later observed in tests with gaseous fuel using a porous burner to create nominally one-dimensional flames.

text: BRE examined NASA-considered crew atmospheres: 14.7 psia / 21% O2, 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 and 8.2 psia / 34% O2.
quote: NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.

text: BRE observed quasi-steady burning emulating PMMA and Nylon in microgravity without any air flow, although turning off ventilation is an established step for spacecraft fires.
quote: Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires.

text: Ongoing burning without air flow was seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres being considered for future spacecraft, while such flames in 21% oxygen self-extinguished quickly.
quote: The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.

text: Preliminary BRE results suggest NASA may want to increase use of flammability Test 2 (cone calorimeter).
quote: they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter

text: BRE flight tests used CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter.
quote: Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter.

text: BRE assumes four properties (heat of combustion, heat of gasification, surface temperature, laminar smoke point) define a condensed fuel's steady burning rate.
quote: Four properties, including the heat of combustion, the heat of gasification, the surface temperature, and the laminar smoke point, are assumed to be sufficient to define the steady burning rate of a condensed-phase fuel.

text: In 5-s drop tests a higher-than-theory burning rate for the larger BRE burner indicates the significance of gas radiation.
quote: A higher burning rate for the bigger burner as compared to theory indicates the significance of gas radiation.

text: CFI-G sought the conditions for cool diffusion flames of propane, n-butane and n-pentane, in normal and inverse flames.
quote: Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames

text: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of 500-1000 K and were discovered in 2012.
quote: Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012.

text: CFI-G hypothesized cool diffusion flames where lowering flow causes extinction but raising it causes transition to a hot flame, possibly oscillating.
quote: Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.

text: ACME's primary focus is terrestrial combustion; spacecraft fire safety is a secondary objective.
quote: The research is primarily focused on improving practical terrestrial combustion through fundamental microgravity research, where a secondary objective is spacecraft fire safety.

text: Over a thousand ACME flames were ignited after operations began in September 2017.
quote: Over a thousand flames have been ignited since ACME operations began in Sept. 2017

text: Three ACME studies (soot processes, flame dynamics, low-temperature combustion) used porous spherical burners for a nominally 1-D flame.
quote: Three studies of soot processes, flame dynamics, and low-temperature combustion used porous spherical burners yielding a nominally one-dimensional flame structure.

text: E-FIELD Flames applied up to 10 kV between the burner and a circular mesh electrode downstream.
quote: An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.

text: E-FIELD Flames is not conducted to serve space applications, though it might aid future space combustion devices.
quote: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications

text: E-FIELD Flames used methane and ethylene diluted with nitrogen, from highly stable to near-extinction flames.
quote: Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength.

text: Microgravity isolates electric-field effects from buoyancy forces.
quote: This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces.

text: The electric-field study used the coflow burner and a simple gas-jet burner at voltages of either polarity up to 10 kV.
quote: An investigation of electric-field effects also used the same coflow burner as well as a simple gas-jet burner, with a circular electrode mesh, downstream of the burner, at voltages of either polarity up to 10 kV.

text: SPICE studied 526 flames with burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and co-flow from 5.4 to 65 cm/s.
quote: In total 526 flames were studied.

text: SPICE co-flow velocities ranged from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s.
quote: with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s

text: SPICE fuels included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene mixtures.
quote: Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures.

text: Soot dominates the heat emitted from flames in both normal gravity and microgravity fires.
quote: Previous experiments show that soot dominates the heat emitted from flames in normal gravity and microgravity fires.

text: SPICE results were expected to improve flammability criteria for selecting materials for next-generation spacecraft.
quote: improved flammability criteria for selection of materials for use in the next generation of spacecraft

text: SLICE (completed March 2012) microgravity sooting methane coflow flames had lower soot temperatures and higher soot volume fraction than in normal gravity.
quote: The microgravity sooting flames were found to have lower soot temperatures and higher volume fraction than their normal gravity counterparts.

text: From normal gravity to microgravity, soot shifts from the flame centerline to the wings.
quote: The soot distribution tends to shift from the centerline of the flame to the wings from normal gravity to microgravity.

text: SLICE captured more than 4,000 high-resolution images across 13 testing experiments.
quote: More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments.

text: SLICE aimed to determine liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
quote: Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.

text: In microgravity, maximum CH* concentration in SLICE flames increases with coflow velocity but depends weakly on fuel velocity.
quote: in microgravity, the maximum flame CH* concentration increases with the coflow velocity, but it is weakly dependent on the fuel velocity

text: In microgravity flow-tunnel tests, the 1g Upward Limiting Oxygen Index and Maximum Oxygen Concentration exceeded 0g values by up to 4% O2, i.e. fuels burned in 0g at lower O2 than in NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
quote: The 1g Upward Limiting Oxygen Index (ULOI) and 1g Maximum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) are found to be greater than those in 0g, by up to 4% oxygen mole fraction, meaning that the fuels burned in 0g at lower oxygen concentrations than they did using the NASA Standard 6001 Test 1 protocol.

text: Over virtually all spacecraft atmospheres and flows, opposed flame spread is faster than concurrent, especially in normoxic atmospheres.
quote: over virtually the entire range of spacecraft atmospheres and flow conditions, the opposed spread is faster, especially for normoxic atmospheres

text: Spacecraft materials are certified in the worst-case 30% oxygen, 10.2 psia environment, since oxygen concentration is the primary flammability driver.
quote: since oxygen concentration is the primary driver, all materials are certified in the 30% oxygen, 10.2 psia environment

text: At 14.7 psia the Orion cabin O2 cannot exceed 25.6% without potentially invalidating the 30%/10.2 psia material certification for some materials.
quote: the oxygen concentration for the Orion CM at 14.7 psia cannot be set higher than 25.6% without potentially invalidating the materials flammability certification in 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia for some materials

text: In an 8.2 psia / 34-40% O2 environment, 70% of assessed ISS-heritage ECLSS subsystems would need material replacements.
quote: Material flammability presents the most critical hurdle in the 8.2 psia/34-40% O2 environment, where 70% of the assessed subsystems will require material replacements, many of which have yet to be developed.

text: NASA hypothesizes some materials are more flammable in lunar gravity than on Earth, because buoyant flow both supplies oxygen and cools the flame.
quote: The main hypothesis is that some materials burning in Lunar-g are more flammable than on Earth.

text: LUCI produced the first extended-duration (>25 s) combustion tests in simulated lunar gravity on a spinning New Shepard rocket; FM2 on the lunar surface is planned for late 2026.
quote: These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity.

text: Crews turn off ventilation to help extinguish a fire, but surviving flamelets can grow quickly into a large fire when ventilation increases.
quote: However, some flamelets can survive, and our experiments have demonstrated that flamelets quickly grow into a large fire when ventilation increases.

text: Saffire IV/V fires with heat release rates up to 10 kW did not raise average Cygnus cabin conditions to unacceptable levels.
quote: However, despite having heat release rates up to 10 kW, the average vehicle conditions did not rise to unacceptable levels.
